The story achieves a strong balance between interiority and exteriority, resulting in high emotional flexibility. In the first half, the narrator uses interior reflection and memories to establish their complex feelings toward Q—a mix of affection, admiration, envy, and a desire to see his composed exterior crack. In the second half, the story shifts largely to exteriority as the narrator eavesdrops on the dialogue and physical cues (such as pressed toes, opening and closing a notebook, and a daughter refusing a towel) between Q, Lydia, and Q's daughter. The narrator weaves brief moments of introspection into this observable action, allowing the reader to watch Q fail in real-time while simultaneously experiencing the narrator's shifting emotional response from anticipation to a nuanced, mature empathy.
